A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nonlinear Tree-Sliced Wasserstein framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original gradient-flow, CIFAR-10 generation, self-supervised learning, autoencoder, runtime, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds projection-variant comparisons in Tables 9–10 and an operation-runtime benchmark in Figure 6.

M1.justification: The CircularTSW, SpatialTSW, and SpatialSTSW constructions, splitting mechanisms, objectives, and Algorithms 1–3 are retained. The new projection-selection guidance does not introduce another algorithm or establish changes to the existing implementations.

E1.justification: Appendix D.8 substantially broadens Euclidean gradient-flow coverage beyond 25 Gaussians: Table 9 adds Circle, Half Moons, Swiss Roll, and 8 Gaussians. Table 10 adds a distinct synthetic scenario with uniformly distributed L2 norms in dimensions 2000, 5000, and 10000. Existing application coverage remains.

E2.justification: Tables 9–10 newly evaluate SpatialSW and CircularSW alongside the proposed tree variants, SW, and Db-TSW. Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged; the updated citation for TSW-SL does not represent a different baseline.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained. The added Tables 9–10 introduce comparisons using 100 directions, 500 iterations, and the best result across eight learning rates. The new operation benchmark fixes vector dimension at 3000 while varying vector count. These are additional protocols, not revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix D.8 adds substantial analysis of when linear, spatial, or circular projections work best, including a constructed uniform-norm scenario testing the proposed advantage of circular projections. Figure 6 directly benchmarks norms against inner products to investigate runtime efficiency. Existing polynomial-map and line-count ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run gradient-flow averages, standard deviations in Table 7, and ten-run benchmarking in Figure 2. New Tables 9–10 extend the five-run, mean-plus/minus reporting format without introducing a different uncertainty procedure, seed disclosure, or significance test.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 retain their values, but Tables 9–10 add substantial results showing dependence on the data scenario. Db-TSW has the lowest Circle mean in Table 9; Table 10 reports CircularTSW at 0.369 versus SpatialTSW at 314.44 for d=10000. Figure 6 adds operation-runtime findings. These are new-setting results, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the integration domains in Eqs. (5) and (7) from R to R^d and the splitting-map domain in Theorem 4.4 from dimension d to d_theta. These are limited formal corrections; the theorem conclusions and proof arguments in Appendices B–C are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: nonlinear tree projections with injectivity and metric guarantees, Euclidean and spherical variants, and improved empirical performance and efficiency. The new supporting experiments do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix D.8 explicitly states that nonlinear projections need not outperform linear TSW and that selecting a variant requires experimentation. It links circular projections to diverse L2 norms, offers radius-selection guidance, and labels the proposed explanation for diffusion performance as speculation. This substantially expands applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: The abstract newly supplies a public code link. Added material documents the A100 and dimension-3000 operation benchmark and recommends starting radius tuning at 1/sqrt(d) for normalized data. Existing implementation details, application hyperparameters, architectures, and hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 expands citations to Sobolev transport, equivariant networks, and other applications, adds Yamada et al. (2022), and removes Takezawa et al. (2022). Appendix D.8 newly distinguishes projection-based tree methods from clustering-based approaches for generative tasks. The central research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained. Changes include clearer notation explanations, corrected algorithm cross-references and typos, author-affiliation and contribution-note edits, acknowledgements, and the added projection-selection subsection, which shifts subsequent appendix numbering.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 6 and Tables 9–10, enlarges and relocates the existing runtime comparison, and rearranges several floats. Original Figures 6–7 become Figures 7–8 with their content retained. The overall visual design and existing table structures remain similar.

improvement.justification: Tables 9–10 add useful direct nonlinear-SW comparisons and evidence of task-dependent behavior, while Appendix D.8 supplies previously missing selection guidance and qualifications. The code pointer and formal corrections also improve usability. The gain is limited: the added applicability evidence is synthetic, and the unchanged conclusion still broadly claims consistent superiority despite the new qualifications.
